sections.skill: Evaluate claims about AI consciousness and why self-reports do not settle them

questions.prompt: What does "conscious" mean here?

choices.text: Being switched on and connected to electricity, with all of its parts working normally

questions.correct_answer: Having experiences or feelings
questions.intro: Some people claim an AI is CONSCIOUS, meaning it has experiences or feelings. Others say no current AI is. There is no agreed scientific test for consciousness, even for animals, so these claims are hard to settle. One point is widely accepted: a FLUENT SELF-REPORT ("I feel happy," "I am aware") does not settle the question, because language models are trained to produce text like human writing, which is full of such statements. Evaluating a claim means asking what kinds of evidence would count, and noticing when a claim goes beyond the evidence in either direction.

sections.skill: Compare self-reports with a parrot saying "I'm hungry"

questions.prompt: Why might the parrot say "I'm hungry" when it is not?

choices.text: Because parrots always know exactly what they are saying and never repeat sounds by habit

questions.correct_answer: It learned the sound
questions.intro: A parrot trained to say "I'm hungry!" might say it whether or not it is hungry, because it learned the sound. Hearing it does not tell you about the parrot's stomach; you would look at other evidence, such as when it last ate. A language model saying "I feel happy" is similar in one way: the words come from learned patterns, so the words alone do not show what, if anything, is going on inside.

Caution runs both ways: confidently declaring an AI conscious, and confidently declaring that no AI ever could be, both claim more than current evidence supports.
